The word 'bala' affirms what was denied: he will indeed return, and his Lord has always watched him, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari explain. Al-Zajjaj notes that God saw him even before creating him. Readings of 'yuṣallā' differ, and al-Tabari holds that both are correct in meaning.

This verse describes the fate of the one who is given his record behind his back, that is, in his left hand from behind, a sign of humiliation. The commentators explain that he will call out for destruction, crying out 'Woe to me!' and 'Destruction!', and that he will burn in the blaze, meaning he enters Hell and suffers its heat. God gives the reason: he was joyful among his people. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that in this world he lived in comfort and heedlessness, following his desires and never thinking of the Hereafter. Al-Razi adds that he mocked those who believed in the reckoning. The phrase that he thought he would never return is read by the commentators as a denial of resurrection. The word 'yahur' means to return; Ibn Abbas said he did not understand it until he heard a Bedouin woman tell her daughter 'huri', come back. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur take it that he thought he would never return to God, while al-Alusi also offers the weaker reading that he thought he would never return to nothingness. The 'bala' that follows affirms the resurrection: he will surely return, for his Lord has always been fully aware of him, from his creation to his raising.

This passage describes the fate of man on the Day of Resurrection. The one who is given his book behind his back, that is in his left hand in the posture of a humiliated condemned person, will cry out for destruction and burn in the blaze. The commentators explain that this is because he rejoiced among his family in this world, immersed in his desires and heedless of the Hereafter, and he thought he would never return to his Lord or be resurrected. The word 'bala' then affirms that he will return and be raised, since his Lord was watching him and knew his deeds from his creation until his resurrection. The exegetes agree that 'hawr' means returning and that 'zann' means the belief that there is no resurrection. They differ on how the book is handed over behind the back. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Muqatil say the right hand is chained to the neck or the arm is pulled out through the back, while Mujahid simply mentions it being taken from behind, and al-Zamakhshari sees it as a sign of humiliation. The readers differ on 'yusallā': some read it with a doubled lam and others without, and al-Tabari considers both readings correct with the same meaning. Ibn Kathir and others contrast this with the believer who returns joyfully to his family in Paradise after an easy reckoning. Some report that the verses were revealed about Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad and his brother al-Aswad, but their wording is general and applies to anyone who denies resurrection.

In this verse God swears by the twilight, the red glow that remains on the western horizon after sunset. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari, take it to mean this redness, which marks the end of the maghrib prayer time and the start of the night prayer, and this is also the view of the linguists al-Khalil and al-Farra. Abu Hanifa in one of his two reported positions, Abu Hurayra and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, hold that it is the whiteness that follows the redness, while Mujahid and Ikrima say it is the whole day or what remains of it. Al-Tabari considers that the word covers both redness and whiteness, but Ibn Kathir calls the view that it means daytime weak, since the verse links the twilight with the night. The verse then swears by the night and what it gathers, namely animals and creatures that return to their shelter, and by the moon when it is full. The oath supports the statement that people will pass through successive states. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take these as the trials of death, resurrection and judgement; Ikrima speaks of the stages of life from infancy to old age; Sa'id ibn Jubayr describes ranks that raise or lower people according to their deeds. The reading with the second person and a fatha, attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, is applied by several commentators to the Prophet, either as an ascent during the night journey or as a promise of victory. Readers who use the damma, and scholars such as Abu Ubayd followed by al-Tabari, address it to all people. The passage ends with a wonder at the disbelief of those who neither believe nor prostrate when the Quran is recited, announcing a painful punishment, except for those who believe and do good, whose reward will not be cut off.

In this verse God swears by the night and by all that it gathers and covers. The commentators offer several readings of the word wasaqa. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean gathering and collecting: the night brings together the animals and birds that had spread out during the day and shelters them. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report close meanings, such as what it covers with its darkness, what it carries, or what it shelters. 'Ikrima explains it as what it drives back to its resting place, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as the worship done in it, such as night prayer and seeking forgiveness at dawn. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse points to the rest granted to living creatures at night. As for the moon when it is full, the commentators say that it has become complete and bright: Ibn 'Abbas speaks of its perfect shining, Qatada of its roundness, and Ibn Juzayy sees in it the image of light reaching fullness. Together with the twilight, these oaths point to signs that show the power of the Creator.

In this verse God swears by the moon when it becomes full and its light is complete. The commentators explain that the word ittasaqa means to gather, to be complete, to come into order or to become full; this refers to the bright nights when the moon is in its most perfect form. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Qatada report this meaning, and al-Farra' says it happens from the thirteenth to the sixteenth night of the month. The oath follows the verses about twilight and the night, and together they invite reflection on the changes in creation. As for the night that gathers what wasaqa, most scholars, following Mujahid, take it to mean what the night gathers and shelters, such as animals and creeping things; Ikrima takes it to mean what drives everything to its refuge, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr takes it to mean what is done in night prayer and seeking forgiveness. The phrase "latarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq" has been read and interpreted in several ways. With the reading addressed to the Prophet, Ibn Abbas explains it as one state after another, while al-Sha'bi understands heaven after heaven during the night journey. With the plural reading, it addresses all people, who will face the trials of the Day of Judgment state after state. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading while holding that the meaning concerns all humanity. Most exegetes understand tabaq as a state or rank, and 'an as meaning "after". Some see in it the stages of life, from a drop of semen to old age, or the passage from death to resurrection. Others note that these changes show God's power to raise people again. The commentators conclude that the disbelievers refuse to believe despite clear evidence, that God knows what they conceal, and that those who believe and do good will have a reward that never ends.

In this verse God swears by twilight, the red glow that remains on the horizon after sunset, by the night and what it gathers, and by the moon when it is full. He then states the object of the oath: "you will surely pass from state to state" (tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq), each stage matching the one before in hardship and terror. Most commentators read this as "state after state." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Qatada explain that it refers to the stages of human life, from the drop of semen through the embryo, then childhood, youth and old age, and then death, resurrection, judgement and recompense. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also mention the ordeals of death, resurrection and the reckoning, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr sees a movement from station to station, so that those who were lowly in this world are raised in the hereafter and the proud are brought low. Abu 'Ubayda reads it as following the ways of those who came before you. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the plural reading, since the surrounding verses address people in general. The singular reading with a fatha has mostly been understood as addressed to the Prophet: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi take it as ascending from heaven to heaven during the Night Journey, while others see it as a promise of victory and successive conquests. Ibn Mas'ud reports that the heaven itself passes through changing states, at times split open and at times like molten brass. Al-Tabari judges the plural reading to be the soundest, since it covers all people.

God swears here by twilight, by the night and what it gathers, and by the moon when it is full, affirming that people will pass through successive states and trials, one after another. Then comes the rebuke: what prevents these people from believing, and why do they not prostrate when the Qur'an is recited to them? The commentators agree that this is a question of reproach and astonishment, since the evidence is clear. They differ over the meaning of ash-shafaq. Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars take it to be the redness that remains after sunset, al-Mujahid says it is the whole day, 'Ikrima says what remains of the day, and Abu Hanifa, in one of his two reported views, says it is the whitish light. Regarding wa ma wasaq, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain it as what is gathered and joined together, while 'Ikrima explains it as what the night drives back to its shelter. All agree that ittasaqa means the moon becomes complete and full. As for the tabaq through which people are carried, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and al-Hasan take them as successive conditions in this life and the next, Ibn Mas'ud and ash-Sha'bi as one heaven after another, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as stations in which people's ranks are reversed. Some readers recite latarkabanna addressing the Prophet, others latarkabunna addressing mankind. Most commentators take the prostration here to mean humble submission, though al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that some understood it as the prostration of recitation. The exegetes conclude that the disbelievers deny, that God knows what they conceal, and that those who believe will receive an unending reward.

In these verses God swears by the twilight, by the night and what it gathers, and by the moon when it is full, that people will pass through successive states and trials, one after another. He then rebukes the disbelievers for refusing to believe and wonders why they do not prostrate when the Quran is recited to them. The commentators broadly agree on the core meaning: prostration here means submission and humility, while the disbelievers deny and conceal what they harbour within. On the meaning of prostration, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ata, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to mean prayer, whereas Abu Muslim and Qatada take it as humbling oneself and submitting. On the twilight, Ibn Abbas, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and most Companions and jurists, including Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, understand it as the redness after sunset, while Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Abu Hanifa say it is the whiteness, and Mujahid says it is the whole day. Regarding the verb 'tarkabunna', the most common reading addresses the Prophet, and Ibn Abbas explains it as one state after another, al-Sha'bi and Masruq as one heaven after another, and Ibn Mas'ud as the changing conditions of the sky. Other readings address people in general, and al-Hasan explains them as alternating ease and hardship, wealth and poverty, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr speaks of the believer rising and the disbeliever falling in the hereafter. On the prostration of recitation, Abu Hanifa considers it obligatory here, al-Shafi'i considers it recommended, and Malik does not count it among the major prostrations.

This verse says that those who disbelieve deny the Qur'an and the Resurrection, and that God knows what they conceal within their hearts. Mujahid and Qatada take the verb yû'ûna to mean that they hide it in their breasts, while Ibn Zayd understands it as gathering both good and evil deeds, as a container holds what is put in it. Several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, explain that the word 'bashshir' (give good news) is used ironically for a painful punishment. The verse then makes an exception for those who believe and do good deeds. Most exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, treat this exception as disconnected, meaning 'but those who believe', who will have a reward that is neither cut off nor diminished. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy consider it a connected exception, referring to those among them already destined to faith. The phrase 'ghayru mamnun' is explained as not cut off, not reduced, not counted, or not followed by reproach. Ibn Kathir rejects the last sense, since grace belongs to God alone. Ibn al-Qayyim sees in this passage the Qur'anic pairing of a threat and a promise, where a thing is set beside its opposite.

The commentators explain that the verse means God knows best what the disbelievers conceal and gather in their hearts, namely their disbelief and denial, and that He will call them to account for it. Mujahid and Qatada understand the verb yu'un as concealing what is kept in the breast, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the gathering of good and bad deeds, the heart being the vessel that holds them. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir keep to the sense of what they hide of denial in their breasts, whereas az-Zamakhshari also includes what they record of evil deeds in their books. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy report both readings, and al-Alusi allows that the phrase may be a metaphor for concealment. Ibn 'Ashur sees the sentence as a parenthetical warning that God will judge their evil intention, since they know the Quran is true yet feign denial. Most commentators treat the good tidings of painful punishment as ironic, and most read the exception 'except those who believed' as disconnected, although Ibn Juzayy treats it as connected if it refers to those whose faith was already decreed. The commentators broadly agree that the reward that is not cut off means one that is neither diminished nor severed.

In this verse God commands His Messenger to give the disbelievers, who reject the Qur'an and the Resurrection, the news of a painful punishment. The commentators explain that the word "give good news" is used here ironically, since good news normally brings joy, whereas the listeners hear it as a threat. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the disbelievers meant are those who deny the Qur'an and the Resurrection. As for the phrase "God knows best what they conceal", Ibn Abbas takes it to mean what they hide in their hearts, Mujahid what they conceal of their deeds, and Ibn Zayd what they gather of good and bad deeds. Concerning the exception "except those who believed", al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi regard it as a disconnected exception, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Jaza'iri treat it as a connected one, referring to those among them whom God had destined to faith. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say the reward promised to believers who do good is "unending", meaning not diminished or cut off, and Hasan adds that it is free from reproach and harm. Thus the verse sets the threat to the disbelievers against the promise of lasting reward for believers.

This verse from Surah al-Inshiqaq states that those who disbelieve deny the signs of God, that God knows best what they conceal in their breasts or store up in their deeds, and that the Prophet is to give them the tidings of a painful punishment. It then makes an exception for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for whom there is a reward that is not interrupted. Nearly all commentators explain "not cut off" as meaning neither diminished nor cut short. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi hold this view, and al-Qurtubi cites a line of al-Harith ibn Hilliza in support. Al-Hasan al-Basri understands it as a reward not clouded by reproach or harm, and al-Razi lists several converging senses, including no cessation, no bitterness and no shortfall, which he considers best taken together. On the exception, most treat it as disconnected, meaning "but", while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy regard it as connected, referring to those among them who will believe. Ibn Kathir adds that the notion of not bestowing a favour applies only to God, since it is His grace, not the believers' deeds, that admits them to Paradise.
